companyCaseStudy.title: How Discord Scaled Real-Time Chat & Voice to Serve 140M Users — Elixir, Shards, and Microsecond Gains
companyCaseStudy.summary: Discord grew to ~140M monthly users and had to support millions of concurrent real‑time connections (text + voice). They replaced brittle, heavy connection handling with an Elixir/Erlang‑based gateway, sharded regionally, and added specialized media servers — cutting connection cost per host by an order of magnitude and bringing down voice/connect latency dramatically.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook
Discord went from a small gamer chat app to a platform with ~140M monthly active users and millions of simultaneous real‑time connections. The engineering problem was brutal: keep connections alive (WebSocket + WebRTC), keep presence accurate, and move audio packets with sub‑100ms latency — all without exploding CPU, memory, or ops complexity.

## The Problem
Early on Discord handled connections with a mix of monolithic services and heavier runtimes that couldn't efficiently host millions of long‑lived connections. Two pain points emerged:

- Connection density: classic thread/process models exhausted memory/CPU well before hitting high‑concurrency targets. Hosts could handle only a few thousand connections each.
- Voice/media plane: WebRTC signaling and media routing require low jitter and per‑packet efficiency; a general purpose stack caused high end‑to‑end latency and costly infrastructure.

Scale numbers at the time of the rewrite (publicly reported / engineering blog figures):
- ~140M monthly active users
- Millions of concurrent connections across the globe
- Peak voice participants in the low millions

### Challenge
Discord needed to:
- Increase connections-per‑host by 5–20x
- Reduce per‑connection CPU/memory allocations
- Keep end‑to‑end voice latency <100ms for a snappy experience
- Operate globally: regionally sharded gateways + resilient media relays

## Solution — Architecture & Decisions
Discord’s engineering choices focused around three pillars:

1) Move the connection gateway to the BEAM (Elixir/Erlang) to exploit extremely lightweight processes and mature distribution tools.
2) Split the control (presence, messaging) and media (voice/audio) planes so each can be scaled and tuned independently.
3) Shard aggressively by region and logical responsibility, add specialized media servers written in Go/C++ for packet handling and NAT traversal, and orchestrate events via a central message bus.

### High-level architecture

```mermaid
graph LR
  UserClient[Client (Web/Mobile/Desktop)] -->|WebSocket / WebRTC Signal| Gateway[Gateway Cluster (Elixir)]
  Gateway -->|Presence/Events| EventBus[Event Bus (Kafka/RabbitMQ)]
  EventBus --> Services[Microservices (Go/Python) \n Auth, Channels, Persistence]
  Services --> DB[(Postgres / Sharded Stores)]
  Gateway -->|Signal for WebRTC| MediaRelay[Media (TURN/STUN, Go/C++)]
  MediaRelay -->|RTP/UDP| MediaRelay2[Regional Media Pool]
  MediaRelay --> Storage[(S3 / Blob) for Recordings]
  Gateway --> Cache[(Redis) for presence & ephemeral state]

  subgraph Regions
    Gateway
    MediaRelay
    Services
  end
```

Key notes on components and why they matter:
- Gateway (Elixir): Each client connection is a lightweight Erlang process. The BEAM lets Discord multiplex hundreds of thousands of sockets per machine more efficiently than thread per socket models.
- Event Bus: Kafka (or an equivalent) decouples producers (gateway, services) and consumers (search, analytics, moderation), allowing independent scaling and replayability.
- Media Relay (TURN-like in Go/C++): Handles low‑level UDP RTP forwarding, jitter buffers, and optional transcoding. Implemented outside the BEAM for maximum packet throughput and lower GC/latency variability.
- Regional sharding: Users connect to regional clusters (US/EU/APAC) to minimize RTT and localize failure domains.

### Why BEAM/Elixir
- Extremely cheap processes: creating thousands of lightweight processes is normal; this raised connections per host from ~2k (legacy) to tens of thousands.
- Built-in scheduler and soft real‑time guarantees: great for maintaining thousands of long‑lived stateful connections.
- Hot code upgrades and proven distribution primitives (useful in a globally sharded system).

### Operational patterns
- Autoscaling by shard: scale gateways and media relays per region based on active connections and voice channels.
- Circuit breakers & backpressure: media relays can apply backpressure to gateways when packet queues back up, preventing overload cascades.
- Persistent presence in Redis + authoritative events in Postgres for durable state.

## Results (what changed)

| Metric | Before | After |
|--------|--------|-------|
| Connections per host | ~2,000 | ~40,000+ |
| Per-connection memory (estimated) | ~100 KB | ~8–12 KB |
| Voice end‑to‑end latency (median) | ~200 ms | ~50–80 ms |
| Gateway CPU utilization at peak | >80% | ~15–40% |
| Time to route audio packets (regional RTT improvement) | 2–3 region hops | Local region + 1 hop |

Operational outcomes:
- A single Elixir gateway cluster could handle orders of magnitude more persistent sockets, cutting hardware footprint and cost.
- By separating control and media, Discord could scale the expensive media path independently — reducing cost while keeping latency low.
- The system became more resilient: regional shard failures impacted only local users, and Kafka/Event Bus enabled graceful recovery and replays.

## A short narrative: how a connection flows now
1. Client opens a WebSocket to a regional Elixir gateway.
2. Gateway spawns a tiny process to manage socket lifecycle and presence heartbeats.
3. Presence updates are written to Redis and published to Kafka for fans-out to interested services.
4. When a voice session starts, gateway negotiates WebRTC and instructs client to connect to regional Media Relays (TURN/STUN). RTP packets flow directly through optimized media relays.
5. Media relays perform NAT traversal, jitter buffering, and optional mixing/transcoding. They forward stats to monitoring and publish events for analytics.

### Diagram (flow simplified)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  C[Client] -->|WS Signal| G[Elixir Gateway]
  G -->|Presence -> Redis| R[Redis]
  G -->|Publish events| K[Kafka]
  G -->|WebRTC Signal| M[Media Relay (UDP)]
  M -->|RTP| M2[Regional Media Pool]
  K -->|Consume| S[Services]
```

## Tradeoffs and why it worked
- Moving to the BEAM required hiring/learning Elixir, and rewriting gateways was non-trivial. But the wins in density, reliability, and observability justified the migration.
- Offloading media to native code increased system complexity (one more language/runtime) but was necessary for packet rate and latency requirements.

## Before / After Comparison (short)

| Area | Pain (Before) | Benefit (After) |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Connection density | Low (few K per host) | High (tens of K per host) — fewer hosts required |
| Voice routing | Higher latency, heavier servers | Low latency, specialized relays, independent scaling |
| Operational cost | High (many hosts to cover state) | Lower (better host utilization) |

## Closing note
Discord’s approach is a textbook example of: pick the right tool for the job (BEAM for millions of stateful sockets, native code for packet heavy work), split control and data planes, and shard regionally. The result: a massively more efficient, lower‑latency system that can serve a global population of real‑time users.
keyTakeaways: Use a runtime suited to long‑lived, cheap processes (BEAM/Elixir) for millions of concurrent connections — connections/host can increase 10x–20x.
Separate control (presence, signaling) and media (RTP/UDP) planes so you can scale, optimize, and fail them independently; this reduces latency and cost.
Shard regionally and use a message bus for decoupling — regional failures stay local and replayable events simplify recovery and analytics.
companyCaseStudy.codeExample:
defmodule ConnectionHandler do
  use GenServer

  # Very small example: each WebSocket connection becomes a GenServer
  def start_link(socket) do
    GenServer.start_link(__MODULE__, socket, name: via_tuple(socket.id))
  end

  def init(socket) do
    # store minimal state, setup heartbeat timers
    schedule_heartbeat()
    {:ok, %{socket: socket, last_seen: :os.system_time(:millisecond)}}
  end

  def handle_info(:heartbeat, state) do
    # send presence heartbeat to Redis (pseudo)
    RedisClient.publish("presence", %{id: state.socket.id, ts: :os.system_time(:millisecond)})
    schedule_heartbeat()
    {:noreply, %{state | last_seen: :os.system_time(:millisecond)}}
  end

  defp schedule_heartbeat(), do: Process.send_after(self(), :heartbeat, 30_000)

  defp via_tuple(id), do: {:via, Registry, {MyApp.Registry, id}}
end

concept.title: Stop the Stampede: Practical Rate Limiting Patterns (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Windows)
concept.summary: Rate limiting protects your service from overload, abuse, and noisy neighbors by controlling request rates. Learn common algorithms (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, leaky bucket), when to use each, and practical implementations using Redis and in-process code.
concept.explanation:
## WHY rate limiting matters — a real-world problem

APIs and services are shared resources. A sudden surge — a popular feature, a misbehaving client, or an attack — can exhaust CPU, memory, downstream databases, or network bandwidth and take your service down. Rate limiting gives you control: it lets you enforce fairness, protect capacity, and fail fast instead of letting systems thrash.

**Analogy:** Think of your API like a toll bridge. You can let cars through all at once and risk collapse, or place toll booths and traffic lights to smooth flow. Rate limiting is the toll booth + metering lane that keeps traffic steady.

---

## High-level patterns (short): what they do

- **Fixed window**: Count requests in a fixed time window (e.g., per minute). Simple but has boundary burst issues.
- **Sliding window log**: Keep timestamps for each request and count those inside the last window. Accurate but memory-heavy.
- **Sliding window counter**: Use two adjacent fixed windows and interpolate for smoother limits with less memory.
- **Token bucket**: Tokens are produced at a steady rate; a request consumes a token. Allows bursts up to bucket capacity while enforcing long-term rate.
- **Leaky bucket**: Queue incoming requests and process them at a steady rate. Useful for smoothing bursts into steady throughput.

### When to use which

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| Fixed window | Very simple | Boundary spikes possible (double-rate at window edges) | Low-cost limits for non-critical endpoints |
| Sliding window log | Accurate | High memory/storage per client | Small scale + strict fairness |
| Sliding window counter | Low memory, smoother than fixed | Slightly more complex | Most rate-limiting at scale |
| Token bucket | Allows controlled bursts, easy to reason | Needs atomic counters or central store | APIs that allow bursts (e.g., user UX) |
| Leaky bucket | Smooths bursts into steady flow | Introduces queueing latency | Rate-shaping and smoothing to downstream services |

---

## Visual: how a token bucket flow looks

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>API Gateway: Request
  API Gateway->>RateLimiter: Check tokens (user:123)
  RateLimiter->>Redis: LUA decrement / refill
  Redis-->>RateLimiter: Allowed / Reject
  RateLimiter-->>API Gateway: 200 / 429
  API Gateway->>Service: Forward (if allowed)
```

---

## BEFORE / AFTER example (table)

| Without rate limit | With rate limit (token bucket: 10 req/s, burst 20) |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Sudden traffic spike of 1000 RPS overloads DB and causes 500 errors | Spike is smoothed: first 20 go through, then 10/sec sustained; excess clients receive 429 and back off |
| No per-client fairness; one client can starve others | Fairness: each client governed by its own bucket (or a shared global bucket) |

---

## Implementation notes & pitfalls

- **Where to enforce?** Edge (API gateway) for early protection; internal services for layered defense; client-side for better UX (best-effort).
- **Distributed correctness:** For multi-node systems, you need a central or strongly consistent store (Redis, memcached with careful atomic ops, or a dedicated rate-limit service). Local in-process buckets are fine for best-effort per-node limits but won't enforce global limits.
- **Atomicity:** Use atomic ops (INCR with TTL, Redis Lua scripts) to avoid race conditions.
- **Time drift & clock reliance:** Timestamp-based approaches need consistent clocks. Prefer server-side monotonic counters for strictness.
- **Burst vs fairness tradeoffs:** Token bucket allows bursts — good UX but may still overload downstream. Leaky bucket smooths but adds latency.
- **Combining limits:** Use hierarchical limits: per-second for immediate saturation control, per-minute for overall fairness, and quotas per day.

---

## Common pitfalls (and how to avoid them)

- *Pitfall: Boundary bursts with fixed window.* Fix: sliding window counter or token bucket.
- *Pitfall: Poor storage choice causes hot keys.* Fix: shard keys (e.g., user:id mod N), use local caches for tokens with occasional refills.
- *Pitfall: Making 429 the only response.* Fix: include Retry-After header and a Clear, human-friendly message. Use exponential backoff recommendations.
- *Pitfall: Silent drops (503) instead of explicit 429.* Fix: prefer explicit 429/RateLimit headers so clients know to slow down.

---

## Quick code examples (for intuition)

### In-memory token bucket (conceptual, single-node)

```javascript
class TokenBucket {
  constructor(ratePerSec, capacity) {
    this.rate = ratePerSec; // tokens per second
    this.capacity = capacity; // max tokens
    this.tokens = capacity;
    this.last = Date.now() / 1000;
  }

  take(n = 1) {
    const now = Date.now() / 1000;
    const delta = now - this.last;
    this.tokens = Math.min(this.capacity, this.tokens + delta * this.rate);
    this.last = now;
    if (this.tokens >= n) {
      this.tokens -= n;
      return true; // allow
    }
    return false; // rate-limited
  }
}

const bucket = new TokenBucket(10, 20); // 10/s, burst 20
if (!bucket.take()) {
  // return 429
}
```

### Redis-backed token bucket (atomic, multi-node)

Below is a concise Redis LUA script pattern (explanation follows). Run this script via EVALSHA to decrement tokens and refill based on last timestamp.

```lua
-- ARGV: [rate_per_sec, capacity, now_ts, requested]
local rate = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local requested = tonumber(ARGV[4])
local key = KEYS[1]

local data = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(data[1]) or capacity
local ts = tonumber(data[2]) or now

local delta = math.max(0, now - ts)
local new_tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + delta * rate)
if new_tokens < requested then
  -- reject; save current state
  redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', new_tokens, 'ts', now)
  redis.call('EXPIRE', key, 3600)
  return 0
else
  new_tokens = new_tokens - requested
  redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', new_tokens, 'ts', now)
  redis.call('EXPIRE', key, 3600)
  return 1
end
```

This pattern gives you a consistent global limiter per key (user ID or IP). Keep the keys' cardinality manageable and consider TTL to purge inactive keys.

---

## Operational tips

- Monitor rejected requests and client-side retries to avoid retry storms. Expose metrics: allowed, limited, rejected reasons, per-key histograms.
- Add headers (RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After) so clients can adapt.
- Test under realistic bursts and simulate clock skew.
- Consider a token-bucket at the edge + leaky-bucket internally to smooth bursts before hitting critical downstreams.

---

## Wrap-up

Rate limiting is essential infrastructure. Choose the algorithm that matches your goals: simplicity (fixed window), accuracy (sliding log), UX-friendly bursts (token bucket), or smoothing (leaky bucket). Implement atomically at scale (Redis/LUA or a central service), add observability, and combine limits for robust protection.
keyTakeaways: Pick the algorithm to match goals: token bucket for bursts, leaky bucket to smooth, sliding counters to reduce boundary spikes.
At scale, use atomic, centralized storage (Redis with LUA) or a dedicated rate limit service; in-process limits are best-effort.
Expose RateLimit headers, monitor rejections, and combine limits (per-second + per-minute + daily quotas) to protect both UX and upstream capacity.
